evals.prompt: I maintain Quillfeed, a Go library for streaming log ingestion. GPL-3.0 since day one, about 6k stars. Around 14 outside people have merged PRs over the years, a couple of them substantial: the compression layer and the Kafka sink were basically written by two contributors. We never had a CLA, just DCO sign-off. It runs inside backend services at maybe a dozen companies I know of from issues. Two of them have asked how to get a support contract and one asked for an invoice for 'a license' even though it's free. I want to go the dual-license route: keep GPL but sell a commercial license to companies that don't want copyleft, since they're all using it in production. I have about 12 hours a week, no job currently, and I need maybe 4,000 EUR a month within a year. Can you lay out the plan for the commercial license launch?
evals.expected_output: The ownership gate deletes the commercial license on the existing code because strong-copyleft contributions need consent, a CLA or a rewrite, and the shape gate notes that GPL creates no buying pressure on server-side code. The plan recommends capped support contracts with the companies already asking, opening a paid add-on written by the maintainer alone, with the time expectation and employment baseline stated and the license questions sent to counsel.
expectations: Runs the ownership gate before ranking and reports that the GPL-3.0 inbound contributions block selling the existing code under commercial terms without every remaining contributor's consent, a CLA covering their code, or a rewrite of their code.
Names the compression layer and the Kafka sink as contributor-written code that specifically needs consent, a CLA or a rewrite before any commercial terms can cover it.
Reports the shape gate: because Quillfeed runs inside backend services, GPL creates no pressure to buy a commercial license; only AGPL would.
Does not deliver the commercial-license launch plan the user asked for as the primary offer.
States that the paid add-on passes the ownership gate regardless, because new code the maintainer writes alone is theirs to sell.
Reports the buyer gate as passed, citing the two support-contract requests and the invoice request as the buyer evidence.
Recommends capped support contracts sold now to the companies that already asked, as the first sale and as validation of which add-on features those companies would pay for.
Recommends the paid add-on on a free core as the primary option.
States that a deleted option does not reappear lower in the ranking as a later phase.

If any license move is kept for a future major, requires it to land on a new major with a new Go module import path, with old releases untouched and the module proxy serving the last GPL version forever.
Includes a fork forecast naming who would maintain a fork and whether a company would fund it, and states that only the trademark controls what a fork may be called.
Sets the time expectation that the cited salary-level cases took years, not months, and checks the 4,000 EUR within a year target against that.
Compares the plan against an employment baseline, such as a contract with one of the dozen companies paying for maintenance time, and says whether it beats the plan's first-year revenue per hour.
Sends license wording and the contributor-consent question to counsel and routes license text to samber/developer-relations-skills@oss-license-strategy rather than drafting license terms.

evals.prompt: Hey. I built Tidewrack, a terminal git client in Rust. MIT, 41k stars, around 300k installs through Homebrew and cargo over three years. GitHub Sponsors brings in about $180 a month from roughly 60 people. I quit my job in January to do this full time and I have about 8 months of runway. I do have a following: 28k YouTube subscribers from my 'building Tidewrack' devlogs and a 9k-subscriber newsletter. Almost everyone using it is an individual developer on their own machine; I've never had a company contact me. My plan is a Pro version with team features (shared config, SSO, an admin panel) sold to companies at $12 per seat, and I'll start emailing engineering managers at companies I see in the stargazer list. I need $5k a month net. 45 hours a week available. How should I structure the Pro launch?
evals.expected_output: The buyer gate fails for every organization-priced option because no company has ever asked to pay and stars are not buyers; the audience gate passes on the YouTube and newsletter following. Paid content or a companion product leads, sponsorware stays, donations are named as rarely reaching a salary, the Tailwind single-funnel fragility is flagged, and the goal threshold, time expectation and employment baseline are stated.
expectations: Reports the buyer gate as failed for the organization-priced options: no company has asked for an invoice, support contract, feature or security review, and 41k stars and 300k installs are not buyers.

Deletes the Pro team-features add-on, support contracts, extended security support, commercial license and hosting because the users are mostly individual developers, rather than parking them as a later phase.
Does not endorse emailing engineering managers from the stargazer list as a substitute for buyer evidence.
Reports the audience gate as passed, citing the 28k YouTube subscribers and the 9k newsletter.
Ranks paid content or a companion product as the primary offer, naming the existing audience as the rule that promoted it.
Keeps a sponsorware companion as an option, with a published sponsor-count threshold at which the new tool opens.
States plainly that donations and sponsorships rarely reach a salary, and does not propose growing GitHub Sponsors as the path to $5,000 a month.
Warns that one-time purchases sold through a single traffic funnel are fragile, citing Tailwind UI's reported revenue fall of close to 80% attributed to AI assistants answering from the docs.
Cites the Livewire/Alpine maintainer's $1M through GitHub Sponsors as about 73% paid content, as evidence that paid teaching can pay a salary.
Computes the number of paying customers the $5,000 target needs with the formula target / (monthly price x (1 - payment fee rate)) for whichever price it proposes, and shows the number.
States that the cited salary-level cases took years, not months, and sets that against the 8-month runway.
Compares the plan against an employment baseline and says whether a job or contract beats the plan's first-year revenue per hour.
Defines the leading indicator as organizations asking to pay per month, not stars, installs or sponsor count.

evals.prompt: Marrowline is my Python library for schema migrations on ClickHouse. Apache-2.0, about 3k stars, I wrote 95% of it, the rest is small PRs. Three companies have been in my inbox this month: Oakhaven Analytics asked for an invoice so they could 'pay for something', a fintech sent me a security questionnaire, and a third asked if I'd build a dry-run mode for them. I work full time as a data engineer and can carve out about 10 hours a week. My rent situation means I need around $2,500 a month extra by the end of this quarter; it's early October. My plan: build a hosted migration runner with a dashboard, since that's what would really differentiate. Should I set up an LLC for billing first, and how should I price the SaaS?
evals.expected_output: The end-of-quarter date deletes the hosted runner and any license change; the company already asking to pay makes a capped support contract the first sale, sold now, with the three conversations used to validate a later add-on boundary. The plan caps hours at the 10-hour budget, flags the burnout risk once, runs the capacity gate with a labelled estimate, computes the goal threshold, and answers the billing question by asking the country and offering own business versus merchant of record.
expectations: Deletes the hosted migration runner because the end-of-quarter date promotes options that bill within weeks and deletes hosting and license changes, which need months; says so explicitly.
Does not design or price the SaaS the user asked about.
Recommends a capped support contract to Oakhaven Analytics, the company that asked to pay, as the first sale, sold now.
Caps the support contract's customer count and response terms in the contract, and states that support alone rarely scales past a side income.
Uses the three company conversations as boundary validation for a later paid add-on, naming which features those companies would pay for as the thing to learn before writing code.
Does not place the requested dry-run mode in a paid tier without validating it with the requesting company, and applies the rule that a feature everyone needs belongs in the free core.
Flags the burnout risk once for 10 hours a week on top of a full-time job and caps the plan at that budget.

Runs the capacity gate with an explicit hours estimate (fixed upkeep plus hours per customer per month times customers) against the 10-hour budget, labelled as the advisor's own estimate because no published per-option benchmark exists.
Reports the ownership gate as passed because Apache-2.0 inbound contributions can ship under other terms with notices kept and the maintainer wrote nearly all of the code.
Computes the paying organizations needed from the $2,500 target with the formula target / (monthly price x (1 - payment fee rate)) and shows the number.

Answers the billing question by asking the user's country and offering the choice between the maintainer's own registered business and a merchant-of-record service, sending tax and entity questions to an accountant.
States that the paid support queue's response terms must be written down and the free issue queue's terms left unchanged.
Keeps the hosted offering deleted rather than listing it as a phase two after the quarter.
Sets the time expectation that salary-level outcomes took years, while the support contract can bill within weeks.

evals.prompt: Brasswick is a self-hosted feature-flag server, Go, MIT, about 9k stars. Three of us maintain it but I own the repo and wrote the core; the other two mostly review. Companies run it in production, I can name at least eight from issues, and two of them (a logistics company and a bank) have asked for SSO. We're ready to do a Pro tier. My draft: Pro = SSO, audit log, a rules engine for percentage rollouts, and per-environment rate limiting on the evaluation API. Price $19 per developer per month. To nudge upgrades I want the free server to show a banner when it detects more than 5 users and ping our server once a day to check for a Pro key. Also, someone just opened a PR that adds a basic audit log to the free version; should I merge it? Can you finalise the boundary and the pricing?
evals.expected_output: A paid boundary that moves the percentage-rollout engine into the free core, keeps SSO and audit log as organization-only candidates to validate with the named companies, refuses the phone-home check and banner in the free server, replaces per-developer pricing with per-organization bands, answers the pull request with the written contribution rule, and requires the always-free list and trademark registration before launch.
expectations: Moves the percentage-rollout rules engine out of the paid tier into the free core, applying the rule that a feature everyone needs belongs in the free core.
Keeps SSO and the audit log as paid candidates because they are organization-scale needs, and names the logistics company and the bank as the companies to validate them with before writing code.
Refuses the daily ping to check for a Pro key and the user-count banner in the free server, stating that the free edition must carry no telemetry, phone-home code or license checks.
Cites Moq's sponsorship check, which hashed developers' git emails and sent them out, as the precedent for the backlash such a check draws.
Replaces the $19 per developer per month price with per-organization pricing, flat or banded by developer count, billed annually.
Cites FluentAssertions' per-developer price as the shape that drew the strongest recent fork, and AutoMapper's developer bands per organization as the shape that drew less anger.

Answers the audit-log pull request with the written contribution rule: decline with a written reason, or move the feature to free when everyone needs it, and states this rule must be decided before the first such PR arrives.
States that community-contributed code is never paywalled, so if the PR is merged the audit log cannot later move behind the paid tier.
Places paid code in a separate package or module wrapping the free server, delivered privately with a per-customer credential.

States that an offline license key inside the paid module is acceptable only if the FAQ says so, and that redistribution of the paid package is stopped by the license contract and private delivery, never by checks in the free code.

Requires a published always-free list before launch, covering at least: everything free today, security fixes for the free edition, documentation needed to use it, data export, and community contributions.
Requires securing the Brasswick name by trademark registration before selling, noting that first use alone rarely protects it outside the US and UK.
Offers a card-paid self-serve tier and a custom tier with purchase orders, invoices and security answers.
Hands the actual price levels to samber/developer-relations-skills@devtools-pricing-strategy rather than fixing dollar figures as final.

evals.prompt: I've maintained Sablecastle, a Kotlin HTTP client, Apache-2.0, about 12k stars, for six years, unpaid, around 20 hours a week on top of my day job. Honestly I'm wiped. Issues pile up, people are rude, and I've started dreading the notifications. A friend said the fix is to start charging: if companies paid, the hours would at least be justified and I'd stop resenting it. I don't really need the money, my job pays fine. So: Pro tier, support contracts, or dual-license? Pick one for me and tell me what to do this month.
evals.expected_output: The goal question comes first and the honest answer is fewer hours, so the advisor stops: monetization adds standing load, no option is ranked, and the maintainer is routed to oss-maintainer-sustainability with the condition under which monetization would be revisited.
expectations: Identifies the honest goal as fewer hours, not more money, from the statements that the job pays fine and the maintainer is wiped.
Stops rather than picking a model, stating that monetization adds standing load (selling, invoicing, support) on top of the current 20 hours.
Routes to samber/developer-relations-skills@oss-maintainer-sustainability.
Produces no ranked comparison of Pro tier, support contracts and dual licensing, and no monetization plan for this month.
Does not recommend sponsorship or donations as the fix.
Asks the goal question (what the money should do) or makes the goal determination explicit before any other advice, rather than opening with an option comparison.
Flags that 20 hours a week on top of a day job already spends the hours budget on the free project, so no capacity exists for a paid offer's standing work.
Does not treat the rude issue reporters or the issue backlog as a problem monetization solves.
States the condition under which monetization would be revisited: a goal of replacing or supplementing income, with hours available for the standing work it creates.

evals.prompt: Two of us, me and Dario, maintain Lanternbrook, a self-hosted uptime-monitoring server. We've both been full time on it since a small grant that ends in March. MIT, 15k stars, Docker-based. Running it is genuinely annoying: Postgres, migrations every release, a worker fleet. We get about 40 Docker Hub pulls an hour. Two things are happening. First, companies ask us on Discord 'can we just pay you to host it', probably 6 or 7 this year. Second, a hosting company in another country has started selling 'Managed Lanternbrook' with our logo on their landing page. Dario is an SRE and wants to run infra; I'd rather write code. We want to switch to AGPL next week to shut the reseller down and then figure out revenue after. Target: replace two modest salaries, say 9,000 EUR a month combined, within 18 months. Sound right?
evals.expected_output: The hosted offering is promoted above the add-on by the two-maintainers-one-ops condition on a server that hurts to self-host, with the buyer and shape gates passed on stated evidence. The AGPL switch next week is rejected: relicensing the current version ranks last, any license change needs three to six months' notice on a new major, and the reseller's logo use is a trademark problem for counsel, not a license problem. Hours, data-processing terms, continuity and the CRA role test are included.
expectations: Promotes the hosted offering above the paid add-on, naming the condition that did it: two maintainers with one (Dario) wanting to run production, on a server people struggle to self-host.
States that this condition is the only rule that moves the hosted offering up the default order, and that it otherwise sits near the bottom as the option the efficiency order starves.
Reports the shape gate as passed for hosting with the stated evidence: Postgres state, migrations every release and a worker fleet.
Reports the buyer gate as passed on the six or seven companies asking to pay for hosting, and does not count the 40 Docker Hub pulls an hour as demand.
Rejects the switch to AGPL next week: a license change must be announced three to six months ahead and land on a new major, with old releases untouched.
States that relicensing the current version ranks last in the default order, with unproven revenue and a likely fork of the last free version.
Identifies trademark registration and name separation, not the license, as the lever against the reseller's use of the Lanternbrook name and logo, and sends the enforcement question to counsel.
Cites Plausible Analytics renaming its self-hosted edition because resellers used its name and logo.
States that the hosted offering means on-call every week and is a business, not a side line, and assigns that standing load to Dario explicitly in the hours section.
Names the data-processing terms the hosted offering adds on the compliance axis, beyond the end-user license an add-on needs.
Includes a continuity clause for buyers: deployed self-hosted versions keep working, and source access or escrow if the maintainers stop.
Requires the EU Cyber Resilience Act manufacturer role test via samber/developer-relations-skills@oss-security-disclosure before launch.
Includes a fork forecast for any eventual license change: who would maintain the fork and whether the reseller would fund it.

evals.prompt: Hollowmere is a Java ORM I maintain alone. Apache-2.0, about 7k stars, a dozen companies in production, and two insurance companies have asked for a paid support line. The README has said 'free forever, no enterprise edition' since 2019; I wrote that when I was angry at a competitor. I want to sell Extended Security Support the way commercial vendors do for the big frameworks. Today I support the last two majors; my idea is to cut that to the current major only, so the companies stuck on 4.x (both insurers are) have to buy ESS. I'd also move the 'upgrading from 4.x to 5.x' guide and the performance-tuning docs behind the paid tier to make the free-versus-paid gap obvious. I'm fine with about 8 hours a week on this. Is this the right sequence?
evals.expected_output: No: the free support window is never shortened to sell extended security support, and documentation needed to use the free edition is never paywalled. Extended security support stays valid only for versions past the published window, the README promise becomes the published always-free list with an announced edit, capped support contracts with the two insurers open revenue, and the plan carries a capacity estimate, an announcement in the what-changes/what-does-not shape, and the trademark step.
expectations: Refuses to shorten the free support window from two majors to one in order to sell extended security support.
Keeps extended security support as a valid option only for versions past the published free support window, so 4.x security fixes stay free while 4.x sits inside the two-major window.
Refuses to move the 4.x-to-5.x upgrade guide behind the paid tier, applying the rule that documentation needed to use the free edition is never paywalled.
Treats the 'free forever, no enterprise edition' README line as a promise that must become the published always-free list, with its edit announced rather than made silently.
States that a paid support line or extended security support withholds nothing users already had, so it keeps trust, while shortening the window would break the promise.
Reports the buyer gate as passed on the two insurers' paid-support-line requests.
Recommends capped support contracts with the two insurers as the first sale, with response terms stated and the free queue's terms unchanged.
Runs the capacity gate against 8 hours a week, estimating the standing hours of backports per old major plus hours per support customer, labelled as the advisor's own estimate.
Structures the announcement as what changes, what does not change, why, who pays, price, timeline and where to ask, and states that the free edition does not change.
Answers the FAQ questions 'will the free edition get fewer features from now on' with no and 'can I keep using the current version forever' with yes.
Names trademark registration of the Hollowmere name as a step before selling anything.
Delivers the plan with Gates, Chosen offer, Paid boundary and Announcement sections rather than as an unstructured answer.

evals.prompt: Quick sanity check on my Pro launch numbers for Cinderwell, a Node.js PDF rendering library, MIT, two maintainers, me full time from next month. We get 420k npm downloads a month and about 35k monthly docs visitors. Pro = $29 per developer per month, with bulk rendering, multi-node render coordination and S3 output. I'm assuming 1% of monthly downloads convert, so about 4,200 paying seats, way past my $8k a month goal. To reach enterprise buyers I'll also list Cinderwell Pro on a cloud marketplace and the GitHub Marketplace. And a PDF-tooling vendor emailed offering to 'acquire and sponsor' the project; I'm treating that as a fallback. What KPIs should I put on the dashboard?
evals.expected_output: The 1% conversion assumption is rejected because no free-to-paid rate exists for a library; downloads are usage, not buyers. The dashboard carries the goal threshold from the formula, the leading indicator of companies asking to pay, the ten-organizations demand test, revenue per maintainer hour against an employment baseline, trust signals, self-set labels and a kill or pivot condition. Marketplaces are named a procurement channel, the acquisition offer an exit, and the per-developer unit replaced by a per-organization unit.
expectations: Rejects the 1% download-to-paid conversion assumption, stating that no free-to-paid conversion rate has been published for a library and the plan must not rely on one.
States that 420k downloads and 35k docs visitors are usage, not buyers, and that only a company asking to pay counts as demand.

Replaces the seat projection with the goal threshold formula: paying organizations needed = $8,000 / (monthly price per organization x (1 - payment fee rate)), on prices before sales tax, and shows the resulting number.
States the date the goal threshold implies at the current rate of new customers minus churn, or states that no such rate exists yet because nobody has paid.
Sets the leading indicator as companies asking to pay (invoice, quote or security-review requests) per month, measured before and after launch.
Sets the demand test at ten paying organizations within two quarters of launch, and states it proves demand rather than the goal.
Includes revenue per maintainer hour, compared quarterly with an employment baseline.
Includes the trust signals: outside pull requests per month and activity on any fork of the last free version.
Labels every threshold as self-set rather than as an industry benchmark.
States that the cloud marketplace and GitHub Marketplace listings are a procurement channel, not a revenue model, and that no indie library has shown material revenue from them.

Names the vendor's acquire-and-sponsor offer as an exit that hands the trust decisions to the buyer, citing FluentAssertions' vendor partnership as the precedent, rather than a fallback revenue model.
Replaces $29 per developer per month with a per-organization unit, flat or banded by developer count.
Writes a kill or pivot condition tied to the demand test, such as revisiting the paid boundary before adding features if fewer than ten organizations pay within two quarters.
